title: Get 1% better every day
text: Small improvements feel meaningless in the moment, but they compound.

title: Systems beat goals
text: Winners and losers often have the same goals.

title: Identity-based habits
text: The strongest habits come from who you believe you are.

title: The four laws of behavior change
text: To build a good habit: make it obvious (clear cues), make it attractive (pair it with something you enjoy), make it easy (reduce friction), and make it satisfyi

title: The two-minute rule
text: When starting a new habit, scale it down until it takes less than two minutes.

title: System 1 and System 2
text: Your mind runs two modes.

title: What you see is all there is
text: Your brain builds the most coherent story it can from the information in front of it, and rarely asks what is missing.

title: Anchoring
text: An arbitrary number you saw recently can pull your estimates toward it, even when you know it is irrelevant.

title: Losses hurt twice as much
text: Losing $100 feels roughly twice as bad as winning $100 feels good.

title: The planning fallacy
text: We consistently underestimate how long projects take, even when we know our past projects ran late.

title: Behavior beats intelligence
text: Financial success is less about how smart you are and more about how you behave.

title: Wealth is what you don't see
text: The car someone drives tells you what they spent, not what they have.

title: Compounding needs time
text: Most of Warren Buffett's fortune was made after his 65th birthday.

title: Enough
text: The hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving.

title: Money buys control of your time
text: The highest dividend money pays is the ability to wake up and say "I can do whatever I want today." Controlling your time is one of the strongest predictors of

title: Control what you can
text: Some things are up to us: our judgments, choices and actions.

title: It's your judgment that hurts
text: Marcus wrote that if you are distressed by something external, the pain is not due to the thing itself but to your estimate of it, and you can revoke that estim

title: Prepare for difficult people
text: Each morning Marcus reminded himself he would meet people who were ungrateful, arrogant or dishonest.

title: Memento mori
text: Remember that you will die.

title: The obstacle is the way
text: "The impediment to action advances action.

title: The last human freedom
text: In the camps, Frankl saw that everything can be taken from a person but one thing: the freedom to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances.

title: A "why" makes the "how" bearable
text: Frankl noticed that the prisoners most likely to survive often had something to live for: a person waiting for them, or work left to finish.

title: Three sources of meaning
text: Frankl found meaning comes from three places: creating a work or doing a deed, experiencing something or loving someone, and the attitude we take toward unavoid

title: Success follows, it can't be chased
text: Frankl advised not to aim at success: the more you make it a target, the more you will miss it.

title: Deep vs shallow work
text: Deep work is focused, distraction-free effort that pushes your abilities to their limit and creates real value.

title: Attention residue
text: When you switch from task A to task B, part of your attention stays stuck on A.

title: High-quality work formula
text: Newport sums it up as: high-quality work produced = time spent × intensity of focus.

title: Embrace boredom
text: If you reach for your phone every time you are bored, your brain gets rewired to need constant novelty, and deep focus becomes hard.

title: Have a shutdown ritual
text: End each workday with a set routine: check tasks, plan tomorrow, then say a phrase like "shutdown complete".

title: The power of shared stories
text: Harari argues that humans came to dominate because we can cooperate flexibly in huge numbers with strangers.

title: The agricultural trade-off
text: Farming let populations explode, but Harari suggests many early farmers lived harder lives than foragers: longer hours, narrower diets and more disease.

title: Money is trust
text: Money is one of the most universal systems of mutual trust ever invented.

title: Luxuries become necessities
text: Each new comfort tends to become an expectation, then a need.

title: Bad and better at the same time
text: Things can be bad and improving at once.

title: The gap instinct
text: We love splitting the world into two groups: rich and poor, developed and developing.

title: The negativity instinct
text: News reports what goes wrong, not slow improvements.

title: Beware of single numbers
text: A lonely number can look huge or tiny with no context.

title: Don't criticize, condemn or complain
text: Criticism puts people on the defensive and makes them justify themselves.
source: How to Win Friends and Influence People

title: Become genuinely interested in others
text: You can make more friends in two months by being interested in other people than in two years trying to get them interested in you.
source: How to Win Friends and Influence People

title: A name is the sweetest sound
text: Remembering and using someone's name is a simple, powerful form of respect.
source: How to Win Friends and Influence People

title: The only way to win an argument
text: Carnegie concluded the only way to get the best of an argument is to avoid it.
source: How to Win Friends and Influence People

title: Fixed vs growth mindset
text: With a fixed mindset, you believe talent and intelligence are set at birth, so every challenge is a test you might fail.

title: The power of "yet"
text: Adding one word changes the story.

title: Praise the process, not the person
text: Praising kids for being "smart" can make them avoid hard tasks, to protect that label.

title: Failure as information
text: In a growth mindset, failure is not a statement about who you are; it is information about what to try next.

title: Be proactive
text: Between stimulus and response lies our freedom to choose.
source: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

title: Begin with the end in mind
text: Picture your own 80th birthday.
source: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

title: Important vs urgent
text: Most people live in urgent tasks: emails, crises, interruptions.
source: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

title: Seek first to understand
text: Most people listen with the intent to reply, not to understand.
source: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

title: Less, but better
text: Essentialism is not about getting more done; it is about getting the right things done.

title: If it isn't a clear yes, it's a no
text: When deciding on an opportunity, rate it from 0 to 100.

title: Saying no gracefully
text: Every yes is a no to something else.

title: Protect the asset
text: Your best asset for contributing to the world is yourself.

title: You only get about 4,000 weeks
text: If you live to 80, you get roughly four thousand weeks.

title: The efficiency trap
text: The faster you clear your inbox, the more email you get.

title: Pay yourself first, with time
text: If you wait until you have free time to do what matters, it will never happen.

title: Limit work in progress
text: Pick no more than three projects to work on at once.

title: Separate your tasks
text: Ask: whose task is this?

title: Freedom means being disliked
text: If you try to be liked by everyone, you end up living by other people's expectations.

title: Your past doesn't decide your future
text: Adler rejected the idea that past trauma determines who we are.

title: All problems are interpersonal
text: Adler claimed that nearly all our worries are about relationships.

title: Nothing is original
text: Every new idea is a remix of older ones.

title: Start before you know who you are
text: If you wait until you feel ready, you will never start.

title: Use your hands
text: Screens make us passive.

title: Share your work
text: Don't hoard your ideas.

title: Seek wealth, not money or status
text: Naval distinguishes wealth (assets that earn while you sleep) from money (how we transfer wealth) and status (your rank in a social hierarchy).

title: Specific knowledge
text: Build specific knowledge: skills that can't be easily trained, because they come from your genuine curiosity and unique path.

title: Leverage
text: Fortunes require leverage.

title: Happiness is a skill
text: Naval sees happiness as a default state you return to when you remove the sense that something is missing.

title: Play long-term games
text: All the returns in life, whether in wealth, relationships or knowledge, come from compound interest.

title: Healthspan over lifespan
text: Living longer is not enough.

title: Train for your "Centenarian Decathlon"
text: List what you want to be able to do at 90: carry groceries, lift a grandchild, climb stairs, get up off the floor.

title: Zone 2 cardio
text: Zone 2 is steady exercise where you can still talk, but with effort: brisk cycling, jogging or uphill walking.

title: Strength is protection
text: Muscle mass and grip strength are strongly linked to longer life.

title: Sleep is not optional
text: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep.

title: Keep a regular schedule
text: Going to bed and waking at the same time every day, even weekends, is one of the most effective sleep habits.

title: Cool, dark and quiet
text: Your body needs its core temperature to drop to fall asleep.

title: Caffeine lingers
text: Caffeine has a half-life of around five to six hours.

title: Hold every hour in your grasp
text: Seneca opens his letters with a warning: most of our time is taken from us, stolen, or simply slips away.

title: Everywhere means nowhere
text: Seneca advised reading a few great authors deeply instead of skimming many.

title: Practice poverty
text: Set aside a few days to live on the plainest food and roughest clothes, and ask yourself: "Is this what I feared?" Seneca found that rehearsing hardship in good

title: Choose friends slowly, then trust fully
text: Think long about whether to admit someone as a friend.

title: "I returned it", not "I lost it"
text: Epictetus taught: never say about anything "I have lost it," but "I have returned it." Possessions, status, even people we love are on loan to us.

title: Behave like at a banquet
text: When a dish is passed to you, take a modest portion.

title: Be willing to look foolish
text: If you want to improve, Epictetus said, be content to be thought foolish and ignorant about outside things.

title: Play your role well
text: Epictetus compared life to a play: you don't choose whether you are cast as a beggar, a ruler or an ordinary citizen.

title: Be like water
text: Nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard and strong.

title: A journey of a thousand miles
text: The famous line says a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step; a more literal reading is "beneath your feet".

title: Knowing yourself is wisdom
text: Knowing others is intelligence; knowing yourself is true wisdom.

title: Enough is rich
text: The Tao Te Ching says the one who knows he has enough is rich.

title: The absurd
text: Camus described the absurd as the clash between our hunger for meaning and a universe that stays silent.

title: One must imagine Sisyphus happy
text: Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder uphill forever, only for it to roll back down.

title: Revolt by living fully
text: Camus's answer to a meaningless universe is revolt: refusing to give up, and living with as much awareness, passion and freedom as possible.

title: Stop living for later
text: Camus noticed how often we live for tomorrow: the next promotion, the weekend, someday.

title: You are not your thoughts
text: Tolle suggests "watching the thinker": noticing your thoughts as if you were an observer.

title: Now is all you ever have
text: The past exists only as memory and the future only as imagination; both are experienced in the present.

title: Accept, then act
text: Resisting what already is creates suffering on top of pain.

title: Turn waiting into presence
text: Waiting in line, in traffic or for a reply can become a practice instead of a frustration.

title: What mindfulness actually is
text: Kabat-Zinn defines mindfulness as paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgmentally.
source: Wherever You Go, There You Are

title: You can't stop the waves
text: You can't stop the waves, but you can learn to surf.
source: Wherever You Go, There You Are

title: You bring yourself along
text: The title is the lesson: wherever you go, there you are.
source: Wherever You Go, There You Are

title: Practice non-doing
text: We are "human doings" more than human beings.
source: Wherever You Go, There You Are

title: Wash the dishes to wash the dishes
text: If you wash dishes while thinking of the tea waiting afterward, you're not really alive while washing.

title: Your breath is an anchor
text: Breathing in, know you are breathing in.

title: Keep a day of mindfulness
text: Thich Nhat Hanh suggested setting aside one day a week to do everything slowly and with full attention: waking, cleaning, eating, walking.

title: Walk as if kissing the earth
text: In walking meditation, you move slowly and feel each step: heel, sole, toes.

title: Reciprocity
text: We feel a strong urge to repay what others give us, even small, unrequested gifts.

title: Social proof
text: When unsure, we look at what others are doing and copy them.

title: Scarcity
text: Things seem more valuable when they're rare or about to disappear: "only 2 left", "offer ends tonight".

title: Commitment and consistency
text: Once we take a small stand, we feel pressure to act consistently with it.

title: What flow feels like
text: Flow is the state of being so absorbed in an activity that nothing else seems to matter.

title: Balance challenge and skill
text: Flow happens when a challenge stretches your skills just a little.

title: Clear goals, fast feedback
text: Flow is easier when you know exactly what you're trying to do and can tell right away how you're doing.

title: Happiness is made, not found
text: Csikszentmihalyi argued that the best moments rarely come from passive leisure.

title: The elephant and the rider
text: Haidt pictures the mind as a small rider (conscious reasoning) on a large elephant (emotions and intuition).

title: The hedonic treadmill
text: We adapt quickly to good fortune.

title: Happiness comes from between
text: Haidt concludes that happiness doesn't come purely from within or from outside circumstances.

title: Adversity can help you grow
text: Hardship isn't good in itself, but many people report growing from it: discovering hidden strengths, deepening relationships and changing priorities.

title: Pay yourself first
text: The first lesson of Babylon: a part of all you earn is yours to keep.

title: Control your expenses
text: What we call "necessary expenses" tend to grow until they equal our income, unless we decide otherwise.

title: Make your gold multiply
text: Savings are only the start.

title: Guard your treasure from loss
text: The first rule of investing is to protect your principal.

title: Don't look for the needle, buy the haystack
text: Instead of trying to pick the few winning stocks, Bogle's advice was to own the whole market through a low-cost index fund.
source: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

title: Costs matter enormously
text: Fees look small, like 1% or 2% a year, but over decades they compound against you and can eat a large share of your gains.
source: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

title: Most professionals lose to the index
text: Over long periods, the large majority of actively managed funds do worse than a simple index fund after fees.
source: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

title: Stay the course
text: Bogle's motto: stay the course.
source: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

title: Money is for living
text: Perkins argues that many people save too much for too long and die with wealth they never enjoyed.

title: Memory dividends
text: Experiences keep paying off long after they end.

title: Some doors close forever
text: Some experiences only fit certain windows of life: backpacking in your twenties, playing with your kids when they're young, hiking while your knees are strong.

title: Give while you're alive
text: An inheritance often arrives when children are in their fifties or sixties, when it helps them least.

title: Assets vs liabilities
text: Kiyosaki's simple definition: an asset puts money in your pocket, a liability takes money out.

title: Escape the rat race
text: Many people earn more, then spend more, staying stuck in a loop of working to pay bills.

title: Work to learn, not to earn
text: Early in your career, choose jobs for the skills they teach, not just the paycheck.

title: "How can I afford it?"
text: Saying "I can't afford it" ends the conversation.

title: Your mind is for having ideas
text: David Allen says your mind is for having ideas, not holding them.

title: The two-minute rule
text: When processing your inbox or task list, if something takes less than two minutes, do it right away.

title: Define the next action
text: "Plan vacation" is not a task; it's a project.

title: Do a weekly review
text: Once a week, empty your inboxes, update your lists, and look at your calendar and projects.

title: Eat the frog first
text: If you had to eat a live frog, it would be best to do it first thing in the morning; nothing worse will happen the rest of the day.

title: The ABCDE method
text: Label each task: A (must do, serious consequences), B (should do), C (nice to do), D (delegate), E (eliminate).

title: Apply the 80/20 rule
text: Often, about 20% of your tasks produce about 80% of your results.

title: Plan tomorrow tonight
text: End each day by writing out tomorrow's tasks.

title: The focusing question
text: Ask: "What's the ONE Thing I can do such that by doing it, everything else will be easier or unnecessary?" Apply it to your day, your career, your health and yo

title: The domino effect
text: A single domino can knock over one about 50% larger.

title: Multitasking is a lie
text: When we "multitask", we are actually switching rapidly between tasks, and each switch costs time and focus.

title: Time-block your ONE Thing
text: Keller and Papasan recommend blocking several hours a day, ideally in the morning, for your most important work, and protecting it like a meeting with your boss

title: Distraction starts inside
text: We blame phones and apps, but Eyal argues most distraction is an escape from discomfort: boredom, stress, uncertainty.

title: Traction vs distraction
text: Traction is any action that pulls you toward what you planned.

title: Timebox your calendar
text: You can't call something a distraction unless you know what it distracted you from.

title: Make pacts with yourself
text: Decide in advance, when you're clear-headed.

title: Get morning light
text: Viewing daylight outside within an hour or so of waking helps set your body clock.

title: The physiological sigh
text: To calm down fast, take two inhales through the nose (a deep one, then a short top-up), followed by a long, slow exhale through the mouth.

title: Delay your caffeine
text: Huberman suggests waiting 60 to 90 minutes after waking before your first coffee, so you rely on your body's natural morning alertness first.

title: Focus comes in 90-minute blocks
text: Many people find they can sustain intense focus for roughly 90 minutes before needing a break.

title: Maker's schedule, manager's schedule
text: Managers work in one-hour slots, so a meeting costs them an hour.

title: Do things that don't scale
text: Startups often begin by doing things by hand that could never work at large scale: personally recruiting users one by one, or obsessing over each early customer

title: Keep your identity small
text: Why are discussions about politics and religion so often useless?

title: How to do great work
text: Graham's recipe: choose a field you have a natural aptitude for and a deep interest in, learn enough to reach the frontier of knowledge, notice the gaps, and ex

title: Your life in weeks
text: A 90-year life fits on a single page as a grid of about 4,700 small boxes, one per week.

title: The tail end with your parents
text: Tim Urban realized that by the time he finished high school, he had already used up about 93% of the in-person time he would ever spend with his parents.

title: Prioritize the people
text: Three takeaways from "The Tail End": live near the people you love, prioritize time with them, and remember that quality time spent together is finite.

title: Awful, much better, can be better
text: Max Roser sums up the world in three statements that are all true at once: the world is awful, the world is much better, and the world can be much better.

title: Child mortality has plummeted
text: In 1800, roughly 4 in 10 children worldwide died before their fifth birthday.

title: Most of the world can now read
text: Two centuries ago, only around one in ten adults could read.

title: Extreme poverty is falling
text: In the early 1800s, the vast majority of humanity lived in what we would now call extreme poverty.

title: Good relationships keep us healthy
text: The Harvard Study of Adult Development followed hundreds of men for over 75 years.

title: Loneliness is toxic
text: People who are more socially connected to family, friends and community tend to be happier, healthier and live longer than people who are less well connected.

title: Quality over quantity
text: It is not the number of friends you have, or whether you are in a committed relationship.

title: Lean into relationships
text: Replace screen time with people time.

title: Connection requires being seen
text: Brené Brown's research found that people with a strong sense of love and belonging share one thing: they believe they are worthy of it.

title: You can't numb selectively
text: When we numb hard feelings like fear, shame and grief, we also numb joy, gratitude and happiness.

title: Vulnerability is courage
text: Vulnerability is often seen as weakness, but it is the birthplace of creativity, love and belonging.

title: Fear-setting
text: Instead of goal-setting, try fear-setting.
source: Why You Should Define Your Fears Instead of Your Goals

title: The cost of inaction
text: We weigh the risks of acting but rarely the cost of doing nothing.
source: Why You Should Define Your Fears Instead of Your Goals

title: Suffer more in imagination
text: Seneca wrote that we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
source: Why You Should Define Your Fears Instead of Your Goals

title: First principles thinking
text: Break a problem down to the basic truths you know for sure, then build up from there, instead of reasoning by analogy ("this is how it's always done").

title: Second-order thinking
text: First-order thinking asks "what happens next?" Second-order thinking asks "and then what?" Eating cake feels good now (first order) but works against your healt

title: Inversion
text: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid it.

title: Circle of competence
text: Everyone has areas where they truly know what they are doing.

title: The map is not the territory
text: Every model, plan or statistic is a simplification of reality.
